ev: Root 6-in suckers in water or damp potting mix for a second crop that ripens before frost.
tip: Shade cloth over 95°F helps fruit set. Stake firmly against wind.
Wait for nights above 50°F.
Loves the desert heat. Water deeply, less often.
Plant in blocks of 4+ rows so the wind can pollinate it.
Use intermediate-day or day-neutral varieties such as Candy; short-day types bulb too small here.
Plant cloves in fall; harvest next summer once lower leaves brown.
Give fall transplants afternoon shade for their first 2 weeks of late-summer heat.
Kale sweetens after light frost.

ev: Save seed from your best open-pollinated tomatoes, peppers, beans, squash, sunflowers, zinnias, cosmos and marigolds. Dry fully, then store cool and dark.
tip: Hybrid (F1) varieties won't come true from seed.

ev: Root 4-in tip cuttings in a glass of water; pot up once roots are 1 in long.

tip: Bolts in summer heat. Grow it in spring and fall.

ev: Dig and split clumps into groups of 5–10 bulbs; replant at the same depth.
Take 4-in softwood cuttings, strip the lower leaves and root in gritty mix in bright shade.
Second round: semi-hardwood cuttings root well in late summer. Keep them in a cold frame over winter.
tip: Drought-tough once rooted. Choose hardy rosemary such as 'Arp' or 'Hill Hardy' for cold, windy winters.

ev: Clone from vegetative plants before flowering. Clones count toward the 6-plant limit.
tip: California allows 6 plants per home. San Bernardino County may require a locked greenhouse or other enclosure, so check before planting in open ground. Stake it against the wind.
Plant while dormant. Late-blooming varieties dodge April frosts.

ev: Cut pencil-thick dormant scions and store them wrapped in the fridge.
Whip-and-tongue or cleft graft stored scions as rootstock buds break.
Chip or T-bud when bark slips; unwrap buds after 3 weeks.
tip: Graft apples to apples and stone fruit to stone fruit.
Cover blossoms on nights forecast below 30°F.
Soak the root zone every 7–10 days in summer.
Phelan's cold winters give cherries the chill they need. Plant a self-fertile variety such as Stella or Lapins, and net against birds.
Bloom early and often lose flowers to March frost. Pick late-blooming varieties and plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot.

ev: Stick 10-in dormant hardwood cuttings (2+ nodes) in pots or straight into moist ground.
tip: Native and drought-tough. Prune out old canes in winter. Pick only dark-blue clusters and cook before eating: raw berries, stems and leaves are toxic.
Choose heat-tolerant varieties. They fade once June heat arrives.
Sow before winter rain; they bloom in spring.

ev: Dig and divide crowded daffodil and iris clumps after the leaves die back.
tip: Tulips, daffodils and iris. Gophers eat tulips, so plant them in wire baskets; daffodils are gopher-proof.

ev: Take softwood tip cuttings; lavender and salvia root in 3–4 weeks in gritty mix.

n: Native shrubs (desert willow, apache plume, CA buckwheat)
ev: Collect seed as pods and plumes dry. Desert willow also roots from summer cuttings.
tip: Plant in fall so winter rain roots them. Water every 1–2 weeks the first summer, then only in long dry spells.

n: Native perennials (desert marigold, globemallow, CA fuchsia)
ev: Divide CA fuchsia runners; let desert marigold and globemallow self-sow and move seedlings.
tip: Lean soil, no fertilizer. Cut back by half in late winter.

ev: Pull agave and yucca pups; let cholla joints callus a week before planting. Wear thick gloves.
tip: Choose cold-hardy agaves such as Parry's or Utah agave. Plant in fast-draining soil and water sparingly. Wild Joshua trees are protected, so buy nursery-grown plants.
Fall seeding beats spring. Keep seed moist with short daily waterings until it sprouts. Mow at 3–4 in. Uses more water than anything else on this list.
Water deeply 2–3 times a week before 8 am instead of a little every day.
Needs heat to sprout. Turns brown and dormant after the first frost.

ev: Divide clumps with a spade as new growth starts; keep divisions watered for a month.
tip: Low-water alternative to lawn. Cut deergrass back hard in late winter.
